records.title: Burak Çetin
records.text: The drone now follows me completely autonomously. No GPS, no pilot. 🛸 A few months ago, I shared how I got this custom built quadcopter to hold a rock-solid hover indoors using just LiDAR and optical flow. That was the foundation. Now, the full autonomy stack is live. I’ve built a complete sim-to-real pipeline. The exact same ROS 2 stack that I developed and validated in a Gazebo Harmonic digital twin now flies the real aircraft. Here is what is happening under the hood on the onboard Raspberry Pi 4: - Perception: A live camera feed runs through MediaPipe Pose to extract shoulder landmarks and track the target. - Estimation: A pinhole camera model converts pixel measurements into a metric distance estimate and yaw error. - Control: A custom ROS 2 follow-controller calculates and streams velocity commands to the ArduPilot flight controller via MAVROS. - Fail-safe by design: If any node crashes or the target is lost, the system instantly degrades the aircraft into a safe, altitude-holding hover. The biggest engineering hurdle: Latency. Initially, the drone felt sluggish and overshot turns. Profiling the pipeline revealed the data was almost a second old. By switching QoS to BEST_EFFORT, enforcing latest-frame-only threading, and tuning the EMA filter, I cut the end-to-end latency down to ~240 ms. Now, it tracks where you are, not where you were. I am currently exploring Master's thesis and internship opportunities in Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) for Spring 2027. If your team is tackling similar autonomous challenges, I’d love to connect! For those of you building autonomous systems: what is the most stubborn sim-to-real gap you've ever had to bridge? 👇 #Robotics #ROS2 #AutonomousSystems #ComputerVision #Drones #EmbeddedSystems

For decades it competed on efficiency and won. But efficiency alone no longer protects you when disruption stops being the exception and becomes the operating environment. In my conversations with semiconductor executives this past year, resilience comes up in every boardroom, but almost always framed as a supply chain problem. That instinct is right, but I've come to think it's too narrow. The more useful question isn't "How resilient is our supply chain?" It's "How resilient is our enterprise?" In my latest article, I explore why resilience must extend beyond the supply chain and begin with three critical questions every semiconductor leader should be asking. records.title: Joby Aviation
records.text: When you work at a company building electric air taxis, it is easy to get ahead of yourself telling the story. At Joby Aviation , the future doesn't just happen on the flight line, it takes shape in the narrative we build around it. Spending my time interning with the MarComms team taught me that bringing quiet, zero-emissions flight to the world requires a special kind of bridge, one built out of pixels, story arcs, and authenticity. There’s a clear line between the hardware of aerospace and the "software" of brand building. On one side, you have revolutionary aircraft designed to fundamentally change how cities move. On the other, you have the daily rhythm of digital engagement: writing captions, analyzing audience sentiment, cutting video clips, and finding the exact angle that makes complex technology feel relatable on a smartphone screen. Crafting that bridge taught me a few core lessons about digital storytelling in a revolutionary industry: - Translation over declaration: Highlighting eVTOL specs is easy; making a transformed morning commute feel real to someone on their phone takes translation. - Authenticity anchors trust: When your product sounds like science fiction, hyper-polished PR can feel distant. The raw, human moments behind the tech always resonated most. - Audiences are co-pilots: In an emergent industry like eVTOL, every comment and question builds public trust in real time. Listening is just as vital as broadcasting. Leaving this internship, I’m deeply grateful to the incredible MarComms team at Joby who trusted me to help tell this story. A huge, special shout-out to Max Goldstein for pushing me past my comfort zone every day and showing me how to take complex engineering and give it the sizzle it deserves. Shaping the conversation around the future of flight has been an unforgettable experience, and I'm walking away with a completely reshaped toolkit, invaluable lessons, and a deep appreciation for this team. #JobyAviation #FutureOfFlight #DigitalMarketing #InternshipExperience #SantaCruz #Aviation #Storytelling

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. • Отслеживаете
records.text: During a technical review, I asked to see the training data and validation methodology behind a company's "AI-based multi-sensor classifier." What I got back was a fixed decision tree with manually tuned thresholds — no train/test split, no retraining pipeline, a "confidence score" that was really just a normalized distance metric with no calibration behind it. Here's the part people miss: that's not automatically a bad system. A deterministic, explainable rule-based classifier can be exactly the right architectural choice for a safety-critical decision path — arguably safer than a black-box model in a domain where you'll eventually have to explain your logic to a test pilot or an OT&E board. The actual problem was calling it "AI." That label invites the wrong due-diligence questions — where's your training data, how do you retrain, what's your drift monitoring — and forfeits the credit you'd get for being deterministic and auditable in a domain where explainability is a selling point, not a weakness. How you characterize your own architecture changes which questions you get asked. Answer the right ones on your own terms. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #AI

During a technical review, I asked to see the training data and validation methodology behind a company's "AI-based multi-sensor classifier." What I got back was a fixed decision tree with manually tuned thresholds — no train/test split, no retraining pipeline, a "confidence score" that was really just a normalized distance metric with no calibration behind it. Here's the part people miss: that's not automatically a bad system. A deterministic, explainable rule-based classifier can be exactly the right architectural choice for a safety-critical decision path — arguably safer than a black-box model in a domain where you'll eventually have to explain your logic to a test pilot or an OT&E board. The actual problem was calling it "AI." That label invites the wrong due-diligence questions — where's your training data, how do you retrain, what's your drift monitoring — and forfeits the credit you'd get for being deterministic and auditable in a domain where explainability is a selling point, not a weakness. How you characterize your own architecture changes which questions you get asked. Answer the right ones on your own terms. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #AI

records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of three coequal domains. It isn't. Undersea and space are physical domains. AI and autonomous systems are a technology category. Pairing them isn't redundant; it's the strategy explicitly stating which capability dictates our ability to operate in those specific environments. Both domains share a critical constraint: you cannot assume a reliable link back to a human. A UUV can't surface for a GPS fix, or burst-transmit a position report, without giving away exactly where it is. A satellite, light-seconds from ground control, cannot wait for a human in the loop to execute a dynamic defensive maneuver. In both cases, AI isn't a third priority alongside them — it's the fundamental precondition for the other two working at all. This points to a concrete positioning strategy. If your technical bet is a decision architecture built to operate without a link home — how it resolves conflicting sensor input, operates under uncertainty, and decides when to hold versus act — that architecture doesn't care whether the external physics involve water pressure or orbital mechanics. It's the same class of problem wearing two different sets of physics. Building and selling that decision layer as portable, domain-agnostic IP is what allows a company to sell into both halves of this strategy's hardest domains, rather than getting boxed into a single platform. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope;
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Организация Saildrone разместила контент: WATCH IT HAPPEN: Six months of joint development between Saildrone and Lockheed Martin culminated at the US Navy’s RIMPAC exercise with the first live-fire demonstration in Saild
records.text: Организация Saildrone разместила контент: WATCH IT HAPPEN: Six months of joint development between Saildrone and Lockheed Martin culminated at the US Navy’s RIMPAC exercise with the first live-fire demonstration in Saildrone history. The work began after we announced our strategic partnership in October 2025 to combine Saildrone unmanned surface vehicles with Lockheed Martin’s combat-proven effectors. Teams then worked together to integrate the Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM) launcher onto a Saildrone Surveyor and prepare SD-3001 for the demonstration in Hawaii. Surveyor was already operationally proven. JAGM was already combat-tested. The challenge was to bring the two together quickly and integrate the USV into a Navy fleet environment. During RIMPAC, SD-3001 launched two JAGM missiles while operating in coordination with US Navy assets—the first missile launches from a Saildrone platform. SD-3001 is now well on its way to its next mission. The work with Lockheed Martin continues, with this demonstration helping de-risk larger payload integrations planned for Saildrone Spectre. Read the full story: https://lnkd.in/ejkW2-8N.

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of three coequal domains. It isn't. Undersea and space are physical domains. AI and autonomous systems are a technology category. Pairing them isn't redundant; it's the strategy explicitly stating which capability dictates our ability to operate in those specific environments. Both domains share a critical constraint: you cannot assume a reliable link back to a human. A UUV can't surface for a GPS fix, or burst-transmit a position report, without giving away exactly where it is. A satellite, light-seconds from ground control, cannot wait for a human in the loop to execute a dynamic defensive maneuver. In both cases, AI isn't a third priority alongside them — it's the fundamental precondition for the other two working at all. This points to a concrete positioning strategy. If your technical bet is a decision architecture built to operate without a link home — how it resolves conflicting sensor input, operates under uncertainty, and decides when to hold versus act — that architecture doesn't care whether the external physics involve water pressure or orbital mechanics. It's the same class of problem wearing two different sets of physics. Building and selling that decision layer as portable, domain-agnostic IP is what allows a company to sell into both halves of this strategy's hardest domains, rather than getting boxed into a single platform. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it."
